Chapter 3: The Power of Context—How Environment and Emotions Influence Sexuality
Now that we've explored the dual control model, let’s talk about something just as important—context.
Here’s the thing: sexuality isn’t something that happens in a vacuum. It’s shaped by everything around us—our environment, our emotions, even our relationships. Sometimes, context can quietly support desire and satisfaction... and other times, it can get in the way.
So, what do we mean by context?
Think about the physical setting first. A bedroom filled with clutter, harsh overhead lights, or a door that won’t quite shut? Those little things can act like subtle brakes on desire. But if the room feels cozy, private, and relaxed, it’s so much easier to let your guard down and connect.
Of course, that’s just the physical side. Emotional context matters just as much. When there’s trust, safety, and a real sense of connection, desire has room to grow. But if there’s tension, old arguments lingering, or a sense of insecurity, those can put the brakes on just as quickly.
Let’s break this down a bit:
Physical context factors include things like:
Comfort and privacy—does the space feel safe and inviting? Sensory cues, like soft lighting, the right temperature, or a favorite scent. And, of course, whether there are any distractions or interruptions.
Then there’s the emotional context—the quality of your relationship, how well you communicate, the level of trust, and even your stress or mood on any given day.
Here’s something that surprises a lot of people: for many women, desire is especially responsive to context. In other words, the right environment and emotional climate truly can make all the difference.
Maybe you’ve noticed that desire feels absent at home when you’re stressed or distracted, but suddenly sparks up on vacation, where things feel relaxed and new. That’s not being inconsistent—it’s just being adaptable to the context you’re in.
When you really understand the power of context, it helps clear up a big myth: desire doesn’t always have to be spontaneous. For a lot of people, desire shows up when the right cues and conditions are in place. And that’s completely normal.
So, what can you do to shape your context in a way that supports desire and satisfaction?
Here are a few ideas:
Start by creating a comfortable, welcoming space for intimacy.
Take a moment to address any stress or distractions before you try to connect.
And don’t forget to nurture emotional intimacy—through honest conversations, affection, and shared experiences.
When you pay attention to context, you’re not just waiting for desire to magically appear. You’re creating the conditions that help it grow. And that means being flexible, creative, and working together—rather than getting stuck on rigid expectations.
